meta.title: MCP Question Bank — Chapter 7: Authorization
meta.revision: v2.1 (curated 2026-09-12, 200 items, verified against the 2026-07-28 specification)

questions.question: A client calls a protected MCP server with no token. What comes back, and what does the client do with it?

options.text: 403 with WWW-Authenticate listing required scopes; the client starts a step-up flow
401 with WWW-Authenticate naming resource_metadata; the client fetches that document
200 with an empty result, from which the client infers that authorization is needed
400 with a JSON-RPC error; the client adds the Authorization header and retries

questions.explanation: Missing, invalid or expired tokens all produce 401 plus a WWW-Authenticate header whose resource_metadata parameter points at the RFC 9728 document. 403 is for a valid token with insufficient scope.

questions.question: Your client holds a token with files:read. A write operation returns 403 with scope="files:write". Which scope set should the client request next?

options.text: files:read files:write, the union of what it had and what was challenged
files:write only, since that is what the server said it needs
files:write plus an offline_access scope, so the token can be refreshed
The full contents of scopes_supported, to avoid further round trips

questions.explanation: Scope accumulation is the client's job: it computes the union of previously requested scopes and the challenged ones, so earlier permissions are not lost. Requesting everything in scopes_supported is the fallback only when a challenge carries no scope at all.

questions.question: Which statement about sending access tokens to an MCP server is correct?

options.text: Either the Authorization header or an access_token query parameter
Authorization: Bearer on every request; never in the URI query string
A signed cookie, so browsers can reuse the same credential
Authorization: Bearer on the first request of a session, then a session id

questions.explanation: Authorization MUST be included in every HTTP request from client to server, and access tokens MUST NOT be included in the URI query string. There is no session to attach a credential to after the first request.

questions.question: How should a stdio server obtain credentials for the API it wraps?

options.text: By asking the client for its MCP access token and reusing that token upstream
Through URL-mode elicitation on every single call that needs the upstream API
Through the same OAuth 2.1 flow as HTTP servers, using a loopback redirect URI on the host
From its environment: stdio implementations SHOULD NOT follow the authorization spec

questions.explanation: Authorization is defined for HTTP transports; stdio implementations SHOULD NOT follow it and instead retrieve credentials from the environment. Reusing the client's token upstream would be token passthrough, which is forbidden.

questions.question: Your client fetches the protected resource metadata document named by a 401. What does it get from that document?

options.text: An access token scoped to that resource, ready for use on the very next request it makes
The list of tools the caller is permitted to invoke on that server
The client_id and client_secret the client should use with that resource
The resource identifier and the authorization servers that issue tokens for it

questions.explanation: The RFC 9728 document describes the resource: its canonical identifier and which authorization servers to go to, plus supported scopes. Tokens, client credentials and per-tool permissions are not in it.

questions.question: Mid-session, a call that worked a minute ago returns 401 and the client holds a refresh token. What is the expected behaviour?

options.text: Retry the same token twice before concluding that it has expired
Restart the full authorization code flow, since refresh tokens are not used in MCP
Refresh at the authorization server and retry, without a new user-facing flow
Treat it as a scope problem and request the union of all known scopes

questions.explanation: Expiry is the ordinary case for a 401: exchange the refresh token for a new access token and retry silently. A full interactive flow is the fallback when refresh fails, and scope problems present as 403, not 401.

questions.question: A token is correctly signed by the right authorization server and is not expired, but its aud names a different MCP server. What must the resource server do?

options.text: Accept it but downgrade the request to read-only operations
Reject it with 403, since the token exists but lacks permission here
Reject it with 401: tokens must be issued specifically for this server
Accept it, since the issuer is trusted and the signature verifies

questions.explanation: MCP servers MUST validate that access tokens were issued for them as the intended audience and MUST NOT accept or transit any other token. An invalid token, including a wrong-audience one, gets 401; 403 is about scope, not audience.

questions.question: The authorization server's metadata has no code_challenge_methods_supported field. What must the MCP client do?

options.text: Proceed without PKCE, since the parameter is optional in OAuth 2.1
Proceed, but only for confidential clients holding a client secret
Proceed with the plain code challenge method as a fallback
Refuse to proceed: PKCE support cannot be verified

questions.explanation: Clients MUST implement PKCE and MUST verify support before proceeding. Since neither OAuth 2.1 nor PKCE defines a discovery mechanism, clients rely on that metadata field, and its absence means the client MUST refuse to proceed. S256 is required when technically capable.

questions.question: A client with no prior relationship to an authorization server needs a client_id. Which order does the spec prescribe?

options.text: Pre-registered credentials, then CIMD if advertised, then DCR, then ask the user
DCR first, then CIMD, then any pre-registered credentials, and finally ask the user
Whichever the authorization server advertises; the spec sets no priority
CIMD only: dynamic client registration was removed in 2026-07-28

questions.explanation: The priority is: use pre-registered information if available; use Client ID Metadata Documents if the AS advertises client_id_metadata_document_supported; fall back to Dynamic Client Registration, which is deprecated but not removed; otherwise prompt the user.

questions.question: Which value belongs in the RFC 8707 resource parameter, and where must it be sent?

options.text: The MCP server's canonical URI, in both the authorization and the token request
The client's redirect URI, in the authorization request only
The tool name being invoked, in the token request only
The authorization server's issuer URL, in the token request but not the authorization request

questions.explanation: Clients MUST send the resource parameter identifying the MCP server by its canonical URI, in both requests, and MUST do so whether or not the authorization server supports it. https://mcp.example.com/mcp is canonical; mcp.example.com (no scheme) and URLs with fragments are not.

questions.question: An authorization server advertises authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported: true, but the callback arrives without an iss parameter. What must the client do?

options.text: Proceed, since iss is only a SHOULD in the current revision
Compare the redirect host to the recorded issuer and proceed if they match
Reject the response and stop before redeeming the code
Redeem the code, then verify the issuer from the token's iss claim

questions.explanation: RFC 9207 validation is keyed to that metadata flag: advertised and present means compare to the recorded issuer with an exact string match; advertised and absent means reject. This mitigates mix-up attacks, which PKCE alone does not stop.

questions.question: Dynamic client registration is deprecated and your client has no pre-registered client_id. What is the recommended way to identify it?

options.text: A client_id derived by hashing the redirect URI, as the spec prescribes
A client ID metadata document, whose URL the client presents as its client_id
A self-signed JWT asserting the client's identity, sent in place of a client_id
No client_id at all, since public clients using PKCE do not need one

questions.explanation: The order is pre-registered credentials, then a client ID metadata document (CIMD) whose HTTPS URL is the client_id, then deprecated DCR, then asking the user. PKCE protects the code exchange but does not remove the need to identify the client.
